evidence: Turner explicitly distinguishes an ll extension of śuṣka and cites Oriya sukhilā dried/withered alongside Torwali šugil. These western and central survey sūkh-l/hūk-l adjectives preserve both the dry stem and the l expansion, with ordinary final vowels and western s-to-h outcomes. Compound gone/dried expressions, separate copulas and prefix-bearing forms are excluded; this is a comparative extension-family link, not a detailed reconstruction of every local ending.

Turner lists Punjabi sukkā, Jaunsari sūkhō and the Kullu-area śukkhɔ/śūkho forms under the plain śuṣka dry adjective. These unexpanded survey forms retain that regional stem with ordinary agreement vowels and source sibilant notation. l-bearing expanded adjectives and whole verbal phrases are assigned separately or held.

The sweet branch of mr̥ṣṭa/miṣṭa explicitly gives Assamese miṭhā and Bengali miṭha; the addendum records Assamese phonetic mitha/mita. Hajong mithu therefore fits the eastern sweet series with its source dental spelling and final u, without inventing a separate root from the dental notation.

Turner gives Prakrit titta, Assamese titā and Bengali tita/titā bitter under tikta. Hajong titu preserves this dental t-t bitter stem with regional final u; it is not assigned to the separate retroflex bitter family which Turner discusses as an alternative for Torwali.

Turner explicitly lists Kumaoni rīto and Nepali ritto empty under rikta, and discusses emphatic doubling in Himalayan reflexes. Dotyali rito matches this whole regional empty adjective; the attestation’s short vowel and singleton spelling are preserved.

The first tucchya branch includes Prakrit chuccha, Bhojpuri chũch, Awadhi chũch/chūchā and Hindi chūchā empty. These Dang chucha/cuce forms fit that affricate series and final-vowel variation; the distinct northwestern tuśya branch is not used.
